arch.principle: The whole app rests on two calls: every tool must own its working state, and features of different natures shouldn't share one interaction flow. The first shapes the data structures, the second shapes the UI.
why: Why each tool needs its own state

The first version kept all tool state in one global object: a single inputs and a single parameterValues. The result was that switching tools wiped your selected files, and you couldn't stage two jobs at once. Worse, one long job locked up the entire UI, because every tool shared the same execution entry point. After moving to ToolSession, each of the 53 tools holds its own inputs, parameters, presets, and output directory — switching tools just switches which object is on screen.
Why three categories instead of one flow

'File checksum' needs no output directory, no progress bar, no button — drop a file in and the answer should just appear. But force it through the 'configure → click → queue' flow and the user has to click before seeing anything, then gets asked where to save a file that never gets written. That isn't an implementation problem, it's the wrong abstraction. So we split tools into three categories by whether they produce a file, each with its own interaction.
Why no third-party dependencies

Images, documents, hashing, and compression can all be handled by system frameworks: ImageIO, CoreGraphics, CoreText, PDFKit, Vision, CryptoKit, Compression. Only video encoding/decoding, encrypted 7z volumes, and WebP encoding need external tools. One less dependency layer is one less class of build failure.
Why parameters are described as data instead of hand-written UIs

Each tool declares its own parameter list (type, range, default, visibility condition), and the UI is generated from that declaration. With 53 tools and 189 parameters, hand-writing every form would mean touching three places to add a single parameter. Now a new tool is just a Tool struct.
steps: App launches, all sessions are built
AppState.init walks ToolRegistry.all and creates one ToolSession per tool, 53 in all. It's a lightweight O(53) step that only allocates structs and does no I/O, so launch stays instant.
The user drops in files

The drop lands in DropZone, gets parsed into an array of URLs, and is handed to AppState.addInputs. That does two things: filter out extensions the tool doesn't support, then write into the current session.
Branching: inspector or converter

AppState checks whether selectedTool.inspector exists. If it does, it calls runInspectionIfNeeded() (compute automatically, show inline); if not, it waits for the user to click. This is the dividing line of the whole architecture.
Converters: enqueue and run

Button click → startJob() → resolve the output directory → JobQueue.enqueue(). The queue keeps a pending list and a bounded concurrency limit; jobs run in a Task.detached and never block the main thread.
Summarizing results
When a job finishes, we measure the output size, compute the savings relative to the source files, write the log, then push JobState back to the main thread to update the UI.
pitfalls: Selected files vanish after switching tools
All tools shared one inputs, which select() cleared.
Introduced ToolSession: each tool stores its own, and switching only swaps what's displayed.
Can't do anything else while a long job runs
There was one global execution entry point, so the UI was occupied by the running job.
Jobs go to a background queue, decoupling the UI from the queue; the sidebar shows how many files each tool has staged, so you can move between tools freely.
An inspector tool asks where to save after you click
JobQueue treated 'returned an empty array' as failure, and the output-location setting applied to every tool.
Added ToolResultKind (files / report / inPlace); report tools hide output settings, skip the queue, and show results inline.

pipeline.principle: The hard part of a job pipeline isn't 'calling a command line' — it's three things: concurrency without losing control, cancellation at any moment, and progress that reaches the UI in real time. Those three requirements are why we use ProcessHandle and actor isolation.
why: Why Process instead of a shell

Joining arguments into a string and handing it to /bin/sh invites escaping bugs — spaces, quotes, CJK characters, and parentheses in filenames can all break it. Passing an argument array straight to Process lets the system handle it, and rules out shell injection.
Why ProcessHandle

Process has no graceful cancellation of its own. To cancel a running ffmpeg you need to hold a reference to it so you can call terminate(). ProcessHandle guards that reference with a lock, closing the race where a job is cancelled before the process has even started.
Why progress has to cross threads

ffmpeg's progress is read from a pipe on a background thread, while the UI must be updated on the main thread. Mutating state across threads crashes, so ProgressReporter wraps the callback as @Sendable and JobQueue hops it over to the MainActor.
Why logs are capped
ffmpeg output for a 2-hour video can run to hundreds of thousands of lines. JobLogger caps its buffer at 600 entries (800 for the UI) and drops the oldest, so long jobs don't eat all your memory.
steps: Build the arguments
Each tool is responsible for turning its parameters into a command-line array. This step is a pure function with no side effects, which makes it easy to test.
Start the process
ProcessRunner.run locates the executable (preferring the bundled one), sets environment variables, wires up the stdout/stderr pipes, then calls process.run().
Stream the output
The pipes are read incrementally through readabilityHandler, and LineCollector splits on newlines in a thread-safe way. ffmpeg's -progress pipe:1 emits several key=value lines per second.
Parse progress
Divide out_time_us by the total duration to get a percentage. One gotcha: in some builds the field is called out_time_ms but the unit is still microseconds.
Wait for it to finish
Use withCheckedContinuation to bridge terminationHandler into async, so we don't block a thread.
Commit the result
FileIO.commit picks the destination path according to the conflict policy (rename / overwrite / skip), then swaps it in atomically with moveItem.
pitfalls: The process keeps running after the job is cancelled
When ProcessHandle was marked cancelled before the process started, nothing checked the flag after launch.
On attach(), if it's already cancelled, call terminate() immediately.
The progress bar sits at 0% until the job ends
ffmpeg writes progress to stdout, but we initially routed stderr into the same sink, so the parser was reading log lines instead of progress.
Handle stdout and stderr separately: progress from stdout, logs from stderr.
Leftover temp files
Temp files written during a job weren't cleaned up on the failure path.
Every temp file is covered by defer { FileIO.removeQuietly(temp) }.

ffmpeg.principle: Calling ffmpeg is easy; getting the argument combinations right is not — encoders, containers, pixel formats, and filters carry a lot of implicit constraints, and a bad combination either errors out or produces a file other players can't open.
why: Why arguments are assembled in three layers

Input options (before -i), filters, and output options (after -i) have to be in the right order. Building them as three separate layers avoids 'option in the wrong place' bugs — -hwaccel, for instance, is an input option, and putting it on the output side fails immediately.
Why the container has to match the encoder
The WebM container only accepts VP8/VP9/AV1, and MP4 rejects plenty of combinations beyond VP9. If a user picks H.264 with WebM, we have to correct it automatically or ffmpeg errors out.
Why tools with multiple inputs build -i themselves

The generic wrapper adds an -i input by default. Tools like concat, watermark, and slideshow need several inputs, and if the wrapper adds one more, every input index shifts — -map 1:a points at the wrong stream. That bug actually shipped: concatenating two videos produced 3 seconds instead of 6.
Why text watermarks don't use drawtext

The bundled ffmpeg isn't built with libfreetype, so the drawtext filter doesn't exist. We render the text to a transparent PNG with CoreText and composite it with overlay — which incidentally gives us full CJK font support and better antialiasing.
Why CRF and hardware encoding are handled separately

VideoToolbox doesn't support CRF; it only takes the 0–100 quality scale of -q:v. Mapping CRF onto it is only an approximation, so hardware encoding defaults to off — it's faster, but at the same visual quality the file is noticeably larger.
steps: Pick the encoder
Based on the chosen codec and whether hardware acceleration is on, FFmpeg.videoArgs decides between libx264 and h264_videotoolbox.
Assemble quality arguments
Software encoding uses -crf + -preset; hardware encoding uses -q:v, mapping the CRF value back onto the quality scale.
Stack the geometry filters
Scale, frame rate, and fit mode combine into a single -vf chain. Multiple filters are comma-separated — and note that commas inside a filter expression must be escaped as \,.
Assemble the input side
Multi-input tools supply their own inputArguments; single-input tools use the default ["-i", path].
Run and parse
-progress pipe:1 sends progress to stdout, keeping it separate from the logs on stderr.
pitfalls: Concatenated output is only half as long
The helper added -i input unconditionally, while concat uses -f concat -i list.txt, so the list became a second input and what actually got decoded was the list file itself.
Tools now supply the complete input prefix via inputArguments, and the helper no longer adds one.
Screenshot fails with 'Requested output format png is not known'
The code forced -f png on image output too, but PNG is an encoder name, not a muxer name.
formatHint returns nil for image extensions, letting ffmpeg pick the image2 muxer from the extension.
Watermark fails with 'No such filter: drawtext'
The bundled ffmpeg wasn't built with libfreetype.
Render the text to a PNG with CoreText, then composite with overlay.
Hardware screenshot fails with 'Option hwaccel cannot be applied to output url'
-hwaccel is an input option and had been placed in the output arguments.
Fold it into inputArguments, before -i.

gif.principle: macOS ImageIO can read GIFs but not write them, so GIF output is implemented entirely by hand: color quantization → index mapping → LZW compression → frame composition. This is the closest the project comes to implementing a file format from scratch.
why: Why color quantization is needed

A GIF frame allows at most 256 colors, while a photo has tens of thousands. The colors have to be collapsed onto a single palette. We use median cut: put every color in one box, split it along its longest axis at the median, and repeat until the number of boxes equals the target color count. Each box contributes its weighted average color as one palette entry.
Why a 15-bit histogram instead of full RGB

The full 24-bit color space has 16 million possible values, which would make the histogram array 64 MB. Truncating each channel to 5 bits (32 levels) gives 32768 buckets using only 128 KB, and the eye can barely tell the difference.
Why a lookup table

Each frame has anywhere from tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands of pixels, and every pixel needs its nearest palette color. Walking 256 palette entries per pixel means 33 million distance computations for a single 480×270 frame. So we precompute a 32768-entry lookup table (15-bit color → palette index), after which each pixel costs one array access.
Why we wrote our own LZW

GIF uses variable-code-length LZW, which is nothing like zip's deflate. The system offers no implementation, and we need precise control over when the code length grows and when the dictionary resets.
Why transitions composite pixels by hand

ffmpeg's xfade only works on video streams, while turning a set of images into a GIF means controlling duration and transitions frame by frame. Working directly on the RGBA buffer is more flexible: a fade is linear interpolation, a slide is a coordinate offset, a wipe is a per-column test, and a circular reveal is a radius test.
steps: Decode and normalize the canvas
Each image is rendered onto an RGBA canvas of a single size according to the fit mode (fit / fill / stretch). The canvas size comes from the aspect ratio of the first image.
Build transition frames
Insert a number of intermediate frames between each pair of neighbors. A fade is a·(1-t) + b·t; a slide samples source pixels by x coordinate; a circular reveal compares distance from the center.
Global palette
Sample roughly 220,000 pixels evenly across all frames, run median cut once, and you get one palette shared by the whole animation — far smaller than a per-frame palette.
Index mapping
Use the lookup table to map each pixel to a palette index, with optional Bayer dithering to break up banding.
LZW encoding
Following the GIF rules: emit the clear code first, then extend the prefix pixel by pixel; the code length increases when the dictionary reaches 2^n and resets at 4096.
Write out the 89a structure
Header → logical screen descriptor → global color table → Netscape looping extension → each frame (graphic control extension + image descriptor + LZW data blocks) → trailer.
pitfalls: Visible banding after quantization
Picking the nearest color outright produces stripes in gradients.

Add ordered Bayer dithering: before the lookup, nudge each channel by a small offset from a 4×4 matrix so neighboring pixels land on different palette entries, which the eye blends into a smooth gradient.
Palette color cast
The first version averaged the colors in a bucket without weighting by how often each occurred, so a rare color counted as much as a common one.
Switched to a weighted average based on histogram counts.
Quantization is slow on large images
256 distance computations per pixel.
Precompute a 32768-entry lookup table, bringing the per-pixel cost down to one array access.

markdown.principle: We implement Markdown ↔ rich-text conversion ourselves instead of depending on pandoc. Parsing Markdown is comparatively easy; the reverse direction is the hard part — you have to infer Markdown syntax back out of font traits.
why: Why the Markdown parser is hand-written

Markdown has no single canonical spec, but the syntax people actually use is small: headings, lists, emphasis, code, links, block quotes, tables. A hand-written parser runs about 400 lines — far lighter than pulling in pandoc (a Haskell binary tens of megabytes in size) — and it gives us exact control over the output styling.
Why the reverse direction leans on font traits

What we get out of Word is an NSAttributedString, which carries no "this is a heading" flag, only font information. So the rules are: a font size clearly larger than the body text → a heading; both the bold and italic traits set → ***text***; a monospaced font → backtick code.
Why a paragraph's textLists have to be handled
In rich text a list isn't expressed by a textual prefix — it lives in the textLists of an NSParagraphStyle. Skip that property and you will never detect a list at all.
Why inline parsing needs a single pass

Chaining several regex replacements makes them interfere with each other — after you mark up bold text, the italic regex can match the asterisks you just inserted. A single left-to-right scan that hunts for the matching closing marker as soon as it hits an opening one never processes the same text twice.
steps: Classify each line
Go line by line and decide: blank line, code fence, heading, block quote, bullet list, ordered list, table, or plain paragraph.
Handle code fences
On ```, switch into code mode, buffer every line until the next fence, then emit the whole block in a monospaced font on a grey background.
Parse inline markup
inline() scans for backticks, asterisks, underscores, links, and images, producing the matching attributes for each.
Merge paragraphs
Join consecutive plain lines into one paragraph with spaces — in Markdown a paragraph can span several lines, so emitting line by line gives you broken layout.
Reverse: walk the attribute runs
Use attributes(at:effectiveRange:) to split the text at attribute boundaries, then decide independently which Markdown syntax each run needs.
pitfalls: Markdown exported from Word came out as plain text
We only checked the bold/italic traits and never read the font size, so headings went unrecognized.
Add font-size thresholds: ≥24pt is #, ≥20pt is ##, and so on.
Lists turned into plain paragraphs
We weren't reading NSParagraphStyle.textLists.
Inspect the markerFormat of style.textLists.first and emit - or 1. accordingly.
Text after an inline code span came out with garbled styling
Repeated regex replacement nested the markers inside each other.
Switch to a single-pass scan.

hash.principle: Read the file once and feed five hashers at the same time. This isn't a micro-optimization — on a 4 GB file, reading it five times means four times the disk I/O.
why: Why compute several hashes in one pass

A spinning disk reads sequentially at roughly 150 MB/s, an SSD at roughly 500 MB/s. A 4 GB file takes 8–27 seconds to read once. If the user wants to see both MD5 and SHA-256, computing them separately means reading the file twice. Since we have to read it either way, we may as well feed every hasher in one go.
Why CryptoKit but a hand-written CRC32

CryptoKit offers streaming interfaces for MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256, and SHA-512; they're hardware-accelerated and audited. But CRC32 is a checksum, not a cryptographic hash, and CryptoKit doesn't provide it — so we implement it with a lookup table: 256 entries, one table lookup and XOR per byte.
Why read in chunks
A single Data(contentsOf:) pulls the whole file into memory — a 1 GB file costs 1 GB of RAM. Streaming it in 1 MB chunks keeps memory constant.
Why FileHandle instead of mmap
Memory mapping is more efficient for very large files, but it pins the file into virtual memory and behaves inconsistently on network volumes and external disks. Streaming reads are more predictable.
steps: Open the file and get its total size
The total size is what the progress percentage is computed from.
Loop over 1 MB chunks
For each chunk read, call update(data:) on every hasher in turn. Algorithms that aren't enabled have a nil variable, so optional chaining skips them.
Finish up
finalize() yields the digest, which we turn into a hex string.
Compare (optional)
If the user entered an expected value, compare it against the result for the chosen algorithm, ignoring case.
pitfalls: CRC32 results didn't match the system tools
CRC32 has several variants that differ in initial value, polynomial, and whether the result is inverted. GIF uses a different one.
Adopt the IEEE 802.3 standard: initial value 0xFFFFFFFF, polynomial 0xEDB88320, and an inverted result, which matches zlib.crc32.

inspect.principle: Inspection tools have no buttons. Drop a file in and the result is computed and shown inline; change an option and it recomputes immediately. It's a direct expression of the idea that different kinds of work call for different interactions.
why: Why no button is needed

Computing a checksum or reading image metadata is a pure operation: given the input you get a definite result right away, with no side effects. Making the user click first and then wait for a result is pure overhead.
Why there's a dedicated report model

If we dumped results into the log panel, the user would have to switch to the "Log" tab to see them, and they'd be plain text. Once we define InspectionReport, results can be grouped, carry status, and have a copy button on every row.
Why image detection doesn't go through ffprobe

ffprobe reports a JPEG as a single-frame mjpeg video stream. If we only asked "is there a video stream?", an image would be displayed as "duration 0 seconds, 0 fps, bitrate 0" — all meaningless fields. So we classify by extension first and fall back to stream inspection only when the container is ambiguous (a .mkv, say).
Why debouncing is necessary

Dropping in files triggers a computation, and so does changing a parameter. Flipping the "extract dominant colors" switch repeatedly spawns several concurrent tasks. We compare input snapshots to discard stale results: when a computation finishes, check whether the inputs are still the same batch as when it started, and drop the result if they aren't.
steps: An input change triggers it
addInputs, removeInput, and parametersChanged all call runInspectionIfNeeded().
Mark it as running
Set isInspecting = true so the UI shows a progress indicator.
Compute in the background
Call inspector.inspect(...) inside a Task so the main thread isn't blocked.
Staleness check
Back on the main thread, compare input snapshots and drop the result if they differ, so an old result can't overwrite a new one.
Render
InspectionReportView renders by group; rows with monospaced values get a copy button, and rows with status show ✓ / ✗.
pitfalls: Images showed duration, frame rate, and bitrate
hasVideo only checked videoCodec != nil, and ffprobe treats a JPEG as a video stream.
Introduce MediaKind to classify by extension and add hasTimeline to control whether duration-style fields are shown.
Dropping in a file produced no result automatically
We only computed the estimate and never triggered the inspector.
Call runInspectionIfNeeded() on every path that changes inputs or parameters.

image.principle: Scaling, cropping, rotating, rounded corners, watermarks, and tiling are all implemented with CoreGraphics. The key point is that every geometric operation happens inside a CGContext, rather than producing intermediate files and processing those.
why: Why CoreGraphics instead of ImageMagick

CoreGraphics is a system framework: nothing to install, no inter-process communication, and it can use the GPU and SIMD. ImageMagick adds an extra dependency, and batch processing means launching processes over and over.
Why EXIF orientation has to be handled

A photo taken on a phone stores its pixels sideways and relies on the EXIF orientation tag to tell the viewer how to rotate them. Read the pixels and process them directly and you get a sideways image. So loadOriented reads the orientation tag first and then decides whether to pre-rotate.
Why premultipliedLast

CoreGraphics's premultipliedLast means RGBA with the color channels already multiplied by alpha. It's the most natural format for drawing images into a CGContext; other formats give translucent edges a dark or light fringe.
Why the watermark font size is a percentage of image width

A fixed font size looks completely different across image sizes: 24pt works on an 800px-wide image but is invisibly small on a 4000px-wide photo. Sizing it as a percentage of width keeps the visual proportion consistent across a batch.
Why tiling normalizes the cells first
Stitching together images of different sizes directly gives you a ragged result. Compute a uniform cell size first, scale each image to fit (contain) and center it, then draw on the grid.
steps: Decode and correct orientation
loadOriented reads the EXIF orientation and calls transform to pre-rotate when necessary.
Compute the destination rect per fit mode
resize supports four modes: stretch scales directly; contain/pad scales proportionally and centers (pad fills the background); cover scales up until it covers the target and then crops.
Draw into a new canvas
Create a CGContext at the destination size, set interpolationQuality = .high, then draw.
Encode and write out
ImageIO handles PNG/JPEG/HEIC/TIFF and friends; WebP goes to the bundled cwebp; unsupported formats fall back.
pitfalls: WebP output was a corrupt file
macOS's ImageIO can't write WebP. We first tried writing our own VP8L encoder, but dwebp rejected the bitstream it produced as BITSTREAM_ERROR.
Switch to cwebp (the official WebP encoder) and bundle it plus its 8 dynamic libraries into the app.
Translucent images developed dark edges after compositing
We used a bitmap format with non-premultiplied alpha.
Use premultipliedLast everywhere.

We weren't reading the EXIF orientation.

estimate.principle: The estimate model has two parts: an empirical bits-per-pixel figure for the encoder, and the throughput measured on this machine. Every result is labelled as an estimate and states how it was derived.
why: Why bits per pixel instead of a lookup table

Video size comes down to pixel count × frame rate × bits per pixel, and bits per pixel falls out of the encoder and the CRF. With this model any resolution and frame rate can be derived, with no need to exhaustively test each combination.
Why CRF maps exponentially

CRF and bitrate are roughly exponential — each 6-point drop in CRF doubles the bitrate. So the conversion uses 2^((referenceCRF - actualCRF) / 6), which is far more accurate than a linear approximation.
Why time estimates separate software from hardware encoding

VideoToolbox runs on a dedicated hardware block and is about 5× faster than software encoding. Without that distinction, switching hardware acceleration on would badly overestimate the predicted time.
Why the estimate states its basis
An estimate always carries some error. Rather than hand over a bare number, we tell the user "this is derived from the codec, CRF and resolution" so they can judge how much to trust it.
Why reporting tools show no estimate
"Compute checksum" produces no file, so there is no output size to speak of. Showing "estimated output 1.5 MB" would be misleading, so the estimate card is simply left out.
steps: Read the media info
MediaProbe supplies duration, resolution, frame rate and audio parameters.
Compute the video bitrate
Pixel count × frame rate × bits per pixel. In target-size or explicit-bitrate mode the value you gave is used directly.
Add the audio bitrate
AAC/MP3 uses the bitrate you chose; lossless formats are estimated from sample rate × channels × bit depth; stream copy keeps the source bitrate.
Convert to a size
Total bitrate ÷ 8 × duration, plus 3% for container overhead.
Estimate the time taken
Total frames ÷ local throughput, normalised for resolution and then scaled by the preset and hardware factors.
pitfalls: Estimates were off by too much
The first version used one bits-per-pixel value for every codec, which made HEVC estimates 40% larger than reality.
Calibrate a baseline value per codec.
Target-size compression was estimated inaccurately
It still went through the bitrate model, even though target-size mode specifies the result exactly.
Detect that mode, use the target value directly, and mark it exact rather than estimated.

design.principle: Everything uses macOS semantic system colours and native controls. That gets you automatic light/dark adaptation, increased contrast and the user's own accent colour for free.
why: Why not hard-coded RGB

The first version hard-coded a set of dark values, which forced dark mode, looked out of place on a light system, and ignored the user's accent colour. Switching to labelColor, separatorColor and controlBackgroundColor put the system in charge of all of it.
Why the controls are native

SwiftUI's Slider, Toggle(.switch) and Picker(.segmented) are AppKit controls underneath, so their look, animation and keyboard handling all match the system. Hand-drawn controls rarely get that right.
Why a single spacing scale
Picking numbers like 7, 13 and 19 at random makes an interface look messy. With a scale of 4/8/12/16/20/24/32 every gap is a multiple of 4, and the visual rhythm falls into place on its own.
Why the category colours are desaturated

The 53 tools are spread across 5 categories. Highly saturated category colours would turn the whole sidebar into a rainbow. Instead a desaturated system colour is used only on the icon as a locator cue, never as a large background fill.
steps: Define the semantic colours
Palette maps system colours to names that carry meaning; the UI code only ever refers to the semantic name.
Define the type and spacing scales
Type and Metrics provide the named constants.
Build the components
Section, PrimaryButton, DropZone, FileListView and so on.
The parameter form builds itself
ParameterForm picks the control type from the parameter declaration: a segmented control for a few short options, a pop-up menu for many long ones, and a native switch for booleans.
pitfalls: Text became unreadable after switching between light and dark
It used fixed white or black text.
Switched to the labelColor family of semantic colours.
The button label did not match what happened
Every tool shared a single "Start".
Each tool declares its own verb and can switch it by mode (generate/recognise, encrypt/decrypt, preview/run).

dmg.principle: For a DMG to run straight away on any Mac, two things have to be solved: architecture (it must run on both Apple silicon and Intel) and dependencies (the user must not have to install Homebrew).
why: Why you cannot just copy Homebrew's ffmpeg

Homebrew's ffmpeg links 18 dylibs by absolute path, for example /opt/homebrew/Cellar/ffmpeg/9.0.1_1/lib/libavcodec.63.dylib. On a machine without Homebrew those paths do not exist, and the dynamic linker fails outright.
Why a static build instead

A statically linked ffmpeg depends only on system frameworks (Foundation, VideoToolbox and so on) — zero non-system dependencies. Drop that one file into the app bundle and it runs; no install paths to rewrite and no dependency closure to chase.
Why both architectures are downloaded separately

The static builds are published per architecture. Download one for arm64 and one for x86_64, then merge them into a universal binary with lipo -create. The same app bundle then launches on either kind of Mac.
Why cwebp needs special handling

There is no static cwebp build; it links 8 Homebrew libraries (libwebp, libtiff, libpng, libjpeg and friends). So the whole dependency closure is copied recursively into Contents/Frameworks, and install_name_tool rewrites the references to @rpath.
Why verification uses otool instead of running the binary

Launching a GUI app opens a window and blocks the build script — which is exactly why early builds popped up a window every single time. Instead otool -L statically checks that every dependency resolves.
steps: Download and verify the static tools
fetch-tools.sh downloads them, then checks that the architecture matches and that there are zero non-system dependencies, failing with an error if either check fails.
Build both architectures
Compile once with -target arm64-apple-macosx14.0 and once with -target x86_64-apple-macosx14.0, then merge with lipo.
Embed the tools
ffmpeg/ffprobe are merged into universal binaries; 7z is copied as-is; cwebp is copied together with its dependency closure and its paths are rewritten.
Sign
Sign the embedded binaries and dylibs first and the app bundle last — reverse the order and the outer signature is invalidated.
Verify
Check the app's architecture, that each tool runs, and that every dependency resolves.
Package
hdiutil create produces a compressed read-only image and adds an Applications shortcut.
pitfalls: 7z inside the DMG was only 64 bytes
Homebrew's 7z is a shell wrapper script whose contents are just a path to the real binary. Copying it directly copied the script.
Parse the wrapper script, find the real binary, and copy that instead.
The verification script falsely reported external dependencies in ffmpeg
otool -L on a universal binary prints an architecture header first, in the form path (architecture x86_64):. awk '{print $1}' treated that line as a dependency too.
Only take lines that start with a tab — the real dependency lines.
hdiutil reported "operation not permitted"
Creating a disk image needs permission to mount devices, which a restricted environment denies.
The script detects the failure and prints a clear message plus the manual command, rather than silently producing an empty result.

arch.title: Overall architecture
arch.blurb: Two core decisions shaped the entire project: every tool must own its own working state, and features of different kinds should not share a single interaction flow.

pipeline.title: Job execution pipeline
pipeline.blurb: Between the button click and the file landing on disk come argument building, subprocess execution, progress reporting, and result aggregation. The hard part is not “calling a command-line tool” — it is concurrency control, cancellation, and live progress reporting.

ffmpeg.title: ffmpeg driver and progress parsing
ffmpeg.blurb: Every video feature is built on top of ffmpeg. The difficulty is getting the argument combinations right — encoders, containers, pixel formats, and filters carry a large number of implicit constraints.

gif.title: A GIF encoder built from scratch
gif.blurb: macOS ImageIO can read GIF but not write it, so the entire output path is hand-rolled: median-cut color quantization, LZW compression, Bayer dithering, and per-frame transition compositing.

markdown.title: Two-way Markdown conversion built from scratch
markdown.blurb: No pandoc dependency. It parses Markdown into rich text one way, and infers Markdown syntax back from font traits the other.

hash.title: Five checksums in a single pass
hash.blurb: Read the file once and feed five hashers at the same time. On a 4 GB file that means four fewer trips across the disk.

inspect.title: Inspection tools: drop a file in, get a result
inspect.blurb: Inspection tools have no button, never enter the queue, and never ask where to save — drop a file in and the result appears.

image.title: Image processing core
image.blurb: Resizing, cropping, rotating, rounded corners, watermarks, and stitching all use CoreGraphics — no ImageMagick.

estimate.title: Size and time estimation
estimate.blurb: The model combines empirical bits-per-pixel figures per encoder with throughput measured on the local machine.

design.title: UI design system
design.blurb: Everything uses macOS semantic system colors and native controls, adapting automatically to light and dark mode and to the user's accent color.

dmg.title: Packaging as a universal DMG
dmg.blurb: Making the DMG run on any Mac means solving two problems: architecture (arm64 + x86_64) and dependencies (bundling ffmpeg and its libraries).

video.convert.idea: Transcoding comes down to getting three layers of parameters right: the encoder decides quality and file size, the container decides compatibility, and the two have to agree.
how: Read the target encoder and container extension from the parameters.
Validate the pair: VP9/AV1 can only go into WebM or MKV, so picking MP4 switches the container to WebM automatically; conversely, H.264 with WebM switches back to MP4.
Build the video arguments: software encoding uses -crf + -preset, hardware encoding uses -q:v.
Build the audio arguments: stream copy (-c:a copy) is supported so we skip pointless re-encoding.
For MP4/MOV, add -movflags +faststart to move the index to the head of the file, so playback can start before the whole file has downloaded.
notes: The automatic container correction is deliberate: rather than let ffmpeg fail with a cryptic error, we adjust to what the user actually meant.
Quality defaults to CRF 23 (the sweet spot for H.264) and the preset defaults to medium.

video.compress.idea: Three compression strategies, because they answer three different questions: "how low can the quality go", "how many MB is the hard limit", and "what bitrate do we target".
how: By quality: set CRF directly and let the encoder decide the file size.
By target size: first derive the total bitrate from (target MB * 8 * 1024) / duration, subtract the audio bitrate to get the video bitrate, then approach it with two-pass encoding.
By bitrate: set the average bitrate directly.
Two-pass encoding only makes sense for software H.264 - hardware encoders don't support it - so this branch runs an analysis pass first (writing to /dev/null) and then the real encode.
notes: Target-size mode reserves 2% for container overhead, otherwise the result tends to overshoot slightly.
In two-pass encoding, -pass 1 and -pass 2 must be two separate commands; they can't be crammed into one.

video.resize.idea: Preset sizes scale by height only (keeping the aspect ratio), and only custom sizes need a "fit mode" - a preset is proportional scaling by definition, so "crop to fill" is meaningless there.
how: Preset mode: use scale=-2:H; -2 lets ffmpeg work out an even width for us (most encoders require even dimensions).
Custom mode: work out the target box first, then build the filter according to the fit mode.
Fit uses force_original_aspect_ratio=decrease; fill uses increase followed by crop; stretch just sets the width and height outright.
When "allow upscaling" is off, min(H\,ih) clamps the target to the source dimensions.
notes: Measured: with a 640x360 source and a 480x480 target, fit yields 480x270, while fill and stretch both yield 480x480 (a 63.8% pixel difference).

video.trim.idea: Two ways to trim: re-encoding gives exact cut points, while stream copy is very fast but the cuts have to land on keyframes.
how: Range mode: -ss sets the start and -to sets the end.
When re-encoding, put -ss after -i so the cut is exact.
When stream copying, put -ss before -i so ffmpeg can seek quickly.
Even-split mode uses -f segment together with -segment_time and names the outputs seg_%03d, then submits each one to the destination directory.
notes: In stream-copy mode, add -avoid_negative_ts make_zero; otherwise timestamps can go negative and break playback.

video.concat.idea: Concatenation uses the concat demuxer to read a list file, but joining clips with mismatched parameters goes wrong, so the geometry has to be normalized first.
how: Write a list file with one file 'path' line per clip (single quotes inside the path must be escaped).
Lossless mode is just -c copy - provided every clip has exactly the same encoding parameters.

Re-encode mode: take the first video's resolution as the reference, use scale + pad to bring every clip to the same size, then fps to normalize the frame rate, and finally setsar=1 to normalize the pixel aspect ratio.
notes: The tool has to supply the complete input prefix itself here, otherwise the generic wrapper adds one extra -i and the input indices shift - an early version only emitted the first clip because of this (3 seconds instead of 6).

video.transform.idea: Rotation can either genuinely rotate the pixels with a filter or just write metadata - the latter is instant, but player support is inconsistent.
how: 90 degrees clockwise uses transpose=1, counter-clockwise uses transpose=2, and 180 degrees uses transpose twice.
Mirroring uses hflip / vflip.
With re-encoding off, it writes only the flag via -metadata:s:v:0 rotate=N.

video.speed.idea: Speed changes have to handle video and audio together, and atempo only accepts 0.5-2.0, so anything outside that range has to be chained.
how: Video uses setpts=PTS/speed.
Audio: while the factor is > 2, keep multiplying by 2 and track what's left; while it's < 0.5, keep dividing by 2; then finish with the remainder.
So 8x becomes atempo=2,atempo=2,atempo=2.
notes: With "keep pitch" off, it switches to asetrate, so the pitch shifts with the speed (like fast-forwarding a tape).

video.watermark.idea: The local ffmpeg was built without libfreetype, so there is no drawtext filter; text watermarks are rendered to a transparent PNG with CoreText and then composited with overlay.
how: Measure the real text bounds with CoreText's CTLineGetBoundsWithOptions(.useOpticalBounds), so we don't leave extra whitespace from the font's line height.
Render onto a transparent canvas that fits the text exactly, and write out a PNG.
Feed the PNG in as the second input and composite it with the overlay filter using a position expression.
In the position expression, main_w/main_h are the background dimensions and overlay_w/overlay_h are the watermark dimensions.
notes: The side effect is a bonus: CoreText gives full CJK font support, and its anti-aliasing is better than drawtext's.
Image watermarks control opacity with colorchannelmixer=aa=opacity.

video.screenshot.idea: Single-frame and batch screenshots take two different paths: single frames seek precisely with -ss, while batches pull frames with the fps filter.
how: Single frame: put -ss before -i for a fast seek, plus -frames:v 1 to grab exactly one frame.
Batch: extract with fps=1/interval into a numbered sequence in a temp directory, then rename and submit them in order.
For N evenly spaced shots: work out the range length, divide it by N to get the equivalent interval, then follow the fps path.
JPG quality has to be mapped backwards: ffmpeg's -q:v runs from 2 (best) to 31 (worst), so it's 31 - quality% * 29.
notes: Hardware decoding (-hwaccel videotoolbox) is an input option and must come before -i, otherwise ffmpeg complains that it "cannot be applied to output".

video.frames.idea: Frame extraction uses the select filter with a modulo on the frame number, which is more precise than time-based extraction (no drift from keyframe alignment).
how: Every Nth frame: select=not(mod(n\,N)), which must be followed by setpts=N/FRAME_RATE/TB to rebuild the timestamps.
You can also extract by frame rate: fps=N.
Names can use a sequence number or a timecode (the 00h01m23s456 form, which is safe across filesystems).
There is a "max frames to export" cap, so one wrong click can't dump tens of thousands of images and fill the disk.

video.gif.idea: A high-quality GIF uses a two-pass palette: analyze the whole clip to build a dedicated palette, then quantize with it. Visibly better than a single-pass generic palette.
how: Pass one: palettegen analyzes every frame in the range and writes out a palette PNG.
Pass two: feed the palette in as the second input and quantize with paletteuse.
The chain is fps -> scale(lanczos) -> [reverse] -> palettegen/paletteuse.
Loop count maps onto -loop: infinite = 0, play once = -1, 3 times = 2.
notes: GIF file size grows fast, so the UI suggests keeping clips under 10 seconds.
Dithering is selectable: none / Bayer / Sierra 2-4A / Floyd-Steinberg.

video.fromimages.idea: ffmpeg's image2 demuxer requires consecutively numbered filenames, so the user's files are first copied to canonical names before assembling.
how: Copy the inputs into a temp directory in order, naming them frame_%05d.ext.
Set the input frame rate with -framerate and read the numbered sequence.
"Hold each image for N seconds" translates to a frame rate of 1/N.
For looping playback, split + reverse + concat build a seamless forward-plus-reverse loop.

video.slideshow.idea: Transitions use the xfade filter, but it requires every input to have identical geometry, so each image has to be normalized first.
how: First scale each image to the target resolution, either padding with contain or cropping with cover.
Optional Ken Burns effect: a slow push-in with zoompan.
Each image is its own input and needs -loop 1 -t duration - a still is a single frame, so without looping there is nothing to cross-fade.
Chain them with xfade, accumulating offset by per-image duration - transition duration each time.
notes: Total duration = count * per-image duration - (count-1) * transition duration. Measured: 3 images at 1 second with a 0.6-second transition = 1.8 seconds.
Background music goes in as the last input, with -shortest to match the length.

video.audio.extract.idea: Extracting an audio track and removing one are opposite operations that share a single tool entry point.
how: Extract: add -vn (no video) and pick the encoder for the target format.
Remove: use -c copy -an; the video stream is copied without re-encoding, so it finishes instantly.
The optional "also keep a silent video" writes a second video with the audio track stripped after extracting the audio.

video.audio.merge.idea: Replacing and mixing are two different needs: replacing means "overwrite with the new track", mixing means "play both tracks at once".
how: First split the inputs into a video group and an audio group by extension, and take one from each.
Replace: use -map 0:v -map [a1] and copy the video stream.
Mix: blend the original track and the new one with amix=inputs=2:duration=first.
Volume, delay and fades are strung together into a single audio filter chain.
notes: When the filter chain is empty, anull has to be added, otherwise an empty filter graph is produced and it errors out. This bug fires with the default parameters.

video.cover.idea: Cover art can be an image embedded in the video, or an image exported from one of its frames.
how: Set cover: add the image as the second input, flag it as an attached picture with -disposition:v:1 attached_pic, and copy the video stream.
Extract cover: first ask ffprobe whether an attached_pic stream exists; if it does, take 0:v:1, otherwise take the first frame.
Generate from a frame: seek with -ss and grab one frame.

video.fingerprint.idea: Change the file hash while not re-encoding and not touching the picture, purely by editing metadata and remuxing the file structure.
how: Copy every stream with -c copy, so not a single bit is re-encoded.
Write a random tag into the comment metadata, with optional title randomization.
Add -movflags +faststart to rearrange the container structure, which by itself changes the byte stream.
notes: Verification matters here: before and after the edit, the measured frame count is identical (180 frames), proving the picture really was never re-encoded.

video.strip.idea: Strip private metadata (capture device, GPS, creation time) - again without re-encoding.
how: Clear all metadata with -map_metadata -1.
Optionally keep the rotation info - portrait videos depend on it, and removing it makes them go landscape.

image.convert.idea: The key to format conversion is matching transparency against lossy parameters: JPEG has no alpha, so converting to it gives you a black background.
how: Read the image and correct the EXIF orientation first.
Optionally resize according to the "size handling" parameter.
When the target format has no alpha (JPEG/BMP), lay down a white background before compositing.
Formats ImageIO can write are written directly; WebP goes through the bundled cwebp.
notes: Measured: JPG to WebP drops from 28 KB to 12 KB.
HEIC/AVIF are supported too, but encoding is slower.

image.compress.idea: Target-size compression closes in with a binary search: encoders don't offer a "give me 500 KB" switch, so you have to try.
how: By quality: use the given value as-is.
By target size/percentage: binary search between 0.05 and 1.0, encoding to a temp file and measuring the size each round, up to 7 rounds, stopping early once the error is within 8%.
PNG is lossless, so re-encoding usually makes the file bigger, so it switches to JPEG automatically.
notes: The binary search adds up to 7 extra encodes per image, so batch processing gets noticeably slower - that is the trade-off of precision for time.

image.resize.idea: "Shrink only, never enlarge" is on by default, because upscaling only makes the image blurrier and the file bigger.
how: Compute the target size from the mode: specified width/height, exact size, percentage, or capped long edge.
If shrink-only is on, clamp the target to within the source dimensions.
Redraw with CoreGraphics at .high interpolation quality.

image.transform.idea: Crop first, then rotate - the order can't be flipped, because rotating first changes the coordinate system the proportional crop works in.
how: Proportional center crop: work out the difference between the source and target ratios and take the largest inscribed rectangle.
Percentage inset: pull each of the four sides in by the given proportion.
Rotation uses CGContext's rotate and swaps width and height at the same time.
Mirroring is done with scaleBy(x: -1).

image.stitch.idea: Stitching has to settle on a uniform cell size first, otherwise images of different sizes come out ragged.
how: Horizontal: take the tallest image as the reference and scale the rest to the same height.
Vertical: take the widest image as the reference.
Grid: use the largest width and height as the cell, scaling each image to fit and centering it.
CoreGraphics puts the origin at the bottom left, so row numbers have to be converted top-down: y = total height - (row+1) * cell height - row * spacing.

image.watermark.idea: Watermark parameters are computed as a percentage of the image width, so the visual proportions stay consistent across a batch.
how: Text watermarks are drawn with CoreText; image watermarks are scaled proportionally and then drawn.
Positions use the WatermarkPosition enum; remember that CoreGraphics' origin is at the bottom left when computing them.
Opacity is controlled through context.setAlpha.
notes: Image watermark convention: the watermark image is added as the last file; everything else is an image to process.

image.decorate.idea: Rounded corners, stroke and shadow have to be drawn in the right order: shadow first, then clip and draw the image, then the stroke.
how: Build the rounded-rect path with CGPath(roundedRect:).
Shadow: set the shadow and fill the path (the fill color ends up hidden behind the shadow, leaving only the shadow effect).
Clip to the path before drawing the image, so anything outside the rounded corners is cut away.
Stroke last. When there is a shadow, leave 40px around the canvas, otherwise the shadow gets clipped.

image.gif.idea: A hand-rolled GIF encoder, because macOS can read GIFs but not write them. See the "Hand-rolled GIF encoder" section for details.
how: Decode every frame and render it onto a uniform canvas.
Insert transition frames between adjacent frames.
Sample the whole clip and run a single median cut to get a shared palette.
Map indices through a lookup table, with optional Bayer dithering.
LZW-encode, then write out the GIF89a structure.

image.topdf.idea: Draw page by page with a CoreGraphics PDF context, supporting either "same size as the image" or standard paper.
how: Create a CGContext(consumer:mediaBox:).
With "same size as the image", each page's mediaBox is the image's pixel size.
With standard paper, compute the draw rectangle from the fit mode; for fill, clip to the content area before drawing.
Auto orientation: a landscape image on portrait paper automatically becomes a landscape page.

pdf.toimage.idea: Use PDFKit to rasterize each page at a chosen DPI. The tricky part is the coordinate system: the PDF origin sits in the bottom-left corner, and everything has to be scaled by the DPI factor.
how: Work out the scale factor DPI ÷ 72 (PDF's baseline is 72 DPI).
Create a CGContext at the matching pixel size.
Apply scaleBy then translateBy to map the PDF page coordinates onto the target canvas.
Render and write out page by page.

image.rename.idea: The biggest risk in batch renaming is name collisions — if a becomes b while b becomes c, renaming directly makes the files overwrite each other.
how: Sort the files by the chosen rule and build the complete "source → target" plan.
During execution, rename to a random temporary name first and then to the target name, so chained collisions can't happen.
The template supports {n} for the sequence number, {name} for the original name, {date} for the date, {i} for the original index, and {ext} for the extension.
Preview mode is on by default: it shows the plan without actually renaming anything.

utility.qr.idea: Generate with CoreImage's CIQRCodeGenerator and decode with Vision.
how: Generation: CIQRCodeGenerator produces the QR code, CIFalseColor applies the colors, and the result is scaled up to the target size.
Error correction maps to four levels, L/M/Q/H: the higher the level, the more damage it tolerates, but the denser the modules.
Decoding: VNDetectBarcodesRequest, which covers QR, Aztec, Code128, EAN13, PDF417 and DataMatrix.

utility.rehash.idea: Change a file's hash without changing its contents — append random bytes to the end of the file.
how: Copy the original file, then append N random bytes (in append mode the existing content is left completely untouched).
Recompute the MD5 and record the old and new values to confirm it really changed.
For formats like ZIP and PDF, bytes appended at the end usually don't stop the file from opening normally.
notes: This tool writes files, unlike the read-only "File Checksum" tool — the two are separate. The inspector never modifies any file.

doc.word2pdf.idea: Use CoreText's CTFramesetter to paginate automatically; it's more reliable than working out line breaks by hand.
how: Read the source document into an NSAttributedString.
Create a CTFramesetter and lay out one frame in the page area.
Use CTFrameGetVisibleStringRange to see how much text fit on this page, then continue from there onto the next page until all the text is laid out.
Cap it at 5000 pages so malformed input can't cause an infinite loop.

doc.pdf2word.idea: A PDF's text layer has to be reassembled — the line breaks in a PDF come from layout positions, not from paragraph boundaries.
how: Pull page.string from each page with PDFKit.
Merge -\n (hyphenated line breaks), turn single newlines into spaces, and collapse runs of spaces.
Insert a separator between pages.
When there's no text layer, fail with a clear error and suggest OCR instead of producing an empty document.

doc.txt2word.idea: Line breaks in plain text are hard breaks, so converting them as-is gives you fragmented paragraphs — they need to be merged intelligently.
how: Treat blank lines as paragraph boundaries.
Accumulate non-blank lines in a buffer and only join them into a paragraph (with spaces) once a blank line shows up.
Optional "detect heading lines": short all-caps lines, or lines starting with #, get heading styling.

doc.word2txt.idea: Extract plain text, with an option to keep or drop paragraph breaks.
how: Read the file as rich text, then take .string.
With "keep paragraph breaks" turned off, replace newlines with spaces to get continuous text.

doc.word2md.idea: The reverse conversion infers syntax from font traits. See "Our own bidirectional Markdown converter" for details.
how: Split the text wherever the attributes change.
Font size ≥ 24pt → #, ≥ 20pt → ##, and so on.
Bold + italic → ***; monospaced → backticks; a link attribute → link syntax.
NSParagraphStyle.textLists → list markers.

doc.pdf2md.idea: Same extraction logic as PDF → Word, but the output is Markdown, with a separator between pages.
how: Extract and concatenate the text page by page.
Insert a --- separator between pages.

doc.md2word.idea: Our own Markdown parser renders it into styled rich text.
how: Classify each line: heading, list, blockquote, code fence, table or paragraph.
Parse inline markup in a single pass (bold, italic, code, links, images).
Emit whole code fences in a monospaced font on a gray background.

doc.md2pdf.idea: Render the Markdown into rich text first, then paginate and export to PDF with CoreText.
how: Reuse the Markdown parser to get rich text.
Compute the usable area for A4/Letter/A3 and lay out page by page.

doc.txt2pdf.idea: The same smart paragraph merging as TXT → Word, followed by a PDF export.
how: Merge paragraphs that hard line breaks had split apart.
Optionally detect heading lines and enlarge their font size.
Paginate to the page size.

doc.tortf.idea: RTF is the most compatible rich text format — practically every word processor can open it.
how: Write it out directly with NSAttributedString.data(documentAttributes:).
Fall back to the system's textutil if that fails.

doc.tohtml.idea: Output HTML so it can go straight onto a web page.
how: Generate it with the system HTML writer, keeping the basic styling and links.

doc.toodt.idea: ODT is the open format shared by LibreOffice and WPS.
how: Prefer the system writer; when it isn't supported, route through RTF and let textutil do the conversion.

doc.pdfmerge.idea: When merging PDFs, turn the first page of each source file into a bookmark so you can still jump around quickly afterwards.
how: Create an empty PDFDocument and insert the pages of each source file in turn.
Record the index of each source file's first page and create a PDFOutline node for it.
Attach the nodes to outlineRoot.

doc.pdfsplit.idea: Three ways to split: one file per N pages, one file per page, or extract a specific range.
how: Loop over the page count, creating a new PDFDocument and inserting the matching pages each time.
Name the output files with a part number or the page range.

doc.pdfcompress.idea: Scanned files are big mainly because of the high-resolution images embedded in them, so rasterize each page to a lower-DPI JPEG and put that back in.
how: Work out the scale factor from the target DPI and render each page to a bitmap.
Re-encode at the chosen JPEG quality.
Replace the original pages with the new ones.
notes: Optional grayscale: grayscale JPEGs are much smaller than color ones, which suits text-only scans.

doc.pdfsecurity.idea: Encryption uses PDFKit's write options; decryption requires verifying the password first.
how: Encrypt: set userPasswordOption and ownerPasswordOption, and combine the permission bits from the raw bitmask of PDFAccessPermissions.
Decrypt: verify with unlock(withPassword:), then save a copy.
notes: PDFKit always uses AES-256; the "encryption strength" option in the UI is informational only.
Permission bits have to be combined as raw UInt — Swift bridges that enum as an Optional, so calling formUnion directly won't compile.

doc.ocr.idea: Use Vision's text recognition; it can output plain text, Markdown or a searchable PDF.
how: Rasterize the PDF into a sequence of images at the chosen DPI.
Run VNRecognizeTextRequest on each image.

Searchable PDF: draw the original image, then overlay the recognized text as transparent text at the matching positions — Vision returns normalized coordinates (bottom-left origin), which line up with the PDF coordinate system, so they can be used as-is.

archive.create.idea: Split archives rely on 7z's -v flag, and encryption uses -p together with -mhe=on to encrypt file names as well.
how: Pick the flags by format: -tzip for ZIP, -t7z for 7z.
Splitting: pass a preset size directly (e.g. -v100m); to split by count, estimate the total size first and divide it by the number of parts to get the size of each.
Encryption: -p followed by the password; for 7z, add -mhe=on to encrypt file names too.
Compression level: -mx=0…9.
notes: When splitting by count, estimate the compressed size at 75% — the actual ratio depends on the content and can't be known in advance.
"Store only, no compression" (level 0) suits files that are already compressed and is much faster.

archive.extract.idea: When extracting, the folder name has to lose every archive suffix, otherwise movie.7z.001 ends up in a folder called movie.7z.
how: Strip compound suffixes (.tar.gz and the like).
Strip numeric volume suffixes (.001, .part1).
Strip the single archive suffix (.7z, .zip).
Use -aos to skip existing files, or -aoa to overwrite them.
notes: 7z's error message for a wrong password isn't very informative, so we check whether the output contains the word password and give a clear message like "wrong password, or this archive is encrypted".

utility.hash.idea: One read produces five checksums, so the user doesn't have to pick an algorithm first. See "Computing five checksums in a single pass" for details.
how: Stream the file in 1 MB chunks.
Feed each chunk to MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256, SHA-512 and our own CRC32 implementation at the same time.
Every result line has a copy button.
Paste an expected value to compare against; the UI marks a match with ✓ and a mismatch with ✗.

utility.info.idea: Which image fields get shown depends on the file type — an image has no duration or frame rate.
how: Determine the type from the extension first, and only fall back to ffprobe stream detection when the container is unclear.
Collect the data in five groups: file, dimensions and resolution, color, capture parameters, location.
The dimensions group includes print size: pixel count ÷ DPI converted to inches and centimeters.
Extract 6 representative colors for the dominant palette using median cut quantization.
notes: In practice a single JPEG yields 5 groups and 19+ fields, with no duration, frame rate or bitrate among them.

archive.info.idea: Use 7z l -slt to get a structured key/value listing, then parse out each entry's path, original size and compressed size.
how: Run 7z l -slt and parse by prefixes such as Path = .
Total up the entry count, original size and compressed size, then compute the savings ratio.
Show at most 300 entries in the content list; beyond that, report the total count.

blocks.overview:
Project overview

FormatForge is a native macOS format conversion tool written in SwiftUI, with no third-party Swift packages. Everything runs on your machine, and no data is ever uploaded.

Three kinds of tools, three kinds of interaction

This is the most important design decision in the project. Features of different kinds should not share a single interaction flow:

KindInteractionTools
InspectionDrop in a file and the result appears on its own; no button, no job queue, no save location {", ".join(html.escape(t["name"]) for t in tools if t["isInspection"])}
ConversionPick a preset → tune parameters → click the button → the background queue runs it {sum(1 for t in tools if t["resultKind"] == "files")} tools
In-place editsAct directly on the file itself and produce no new file {", ".join(html.escape(t["name"]) for t in tools if t["resultKind"] == "inPlace")}

Every tool owns its own session

All 53 tools hold their own inputs, parameters, presets, and output directory (ToolSession). Switching tools only switches what is displayed, so you can work on several tools at once — start a long job in “Video Compress”, for example, then switch to “File Checksum” and hash another file.
blocks.quickstart:
Quick start

Just use it (recommended)

Open the DMG and drag FormatForge.app into Applications. The app already bundles ffmpeg, ffprobe, 7z, and cwebp, so you do not need Homebrew or any other dependency.

First launch: the app is not signed with an Apple developer certificate. If macOS blocks it, right-click the icon → choose Open → then click Open again in the dialog. After that you can launch it normally by double-clicking.

Building from source
blocks.architecture:
Architecture overview

The code is split into four layers, and dependencies flow strictly one way: Features → Core → Codecs / Design → App.
blocks.deps:
Dependency notes

The app itself has zero third-party Swift dependencies. Every image, document, hashing, and compression feature comes from a system framework: Foundation, SwiftUI, AppKit, AVFoundation, ImageIO, CoreGraphics, CoreText, PDFKit, Vision, CryptoKit, Compression, and UniformTypeIdentifiers.

Only video encoding, 7z encrypted split archives, and WebP encoding need external executables, and all of them ship inside the DMG.

ToolWhy it is neededWhy not build it ourselves
ffmpegVideo encoding and decoding, filters, muxing Covers hundreds of codecs plus hardware acceleration; reimplementing it is not realistic
7zAES-256 encrypted split archives Has to stay fully compatible with existing archive formats
cwebpLossy and lossless WebP encoding macOS ImageIO can read WebP but cannot write it
One known trade-off: the bundled 7z is arm64. On an Intel Mac you will need to install p7zip yourself if you want encrypted split archives; nothing else is affected.

Testing and verification

The project ships with test.sh, which runs 91 checks against real assets. It verifies behavior, not merely that files exist:

  • After changing the MD5 the frame count is exactly the same — proof that the video really was not re-encoded
  • Split archives must fail with the wrong password and succeed with the right one
  • Compressed video must be smaller (measured reduction: 78%)
  • The GIF must be a multi-frame animation
  • The three fit modes must produce different geometry, so the options are not just for show
  • Chinese file names (including spaces and full-width parentheses) must be preserved exactly
  • Corrupt videos and empty files must be rejected with a clear error
  • All five checksums are compared one by one against the system md5 / shasum / zlib.crc32
  • Dropping in a file must produce a result automatically, with no click required
